title: What I Got Wrong About Pupil Progress Meetings
author: Nickhart
summary: In this reflective piece, school leader mrnickhart revisits the pupil progress meeting model he once believed was well-designed and identifies four structural errors: wrong order of data collection and decision-making, wrong timing, wrong data, and wrong scope. He argues that scheduling meetings around standardised test dates created a false sense of rigour — standardised tests assess national norms, not the curriculum a school has actually taught, making them an unreliable basis for progress conversations. The author admits his model confused "decision-driven data collection" with genuine curriculum-responsive inquiry, and that meetings structured around test matrices were ultimately serving leadership's need for information rather than teachers' need for actionable insight. He concludes by identifying what was worth keeping: rules of thumb for common needs, a solution-focused structure, and a clear mechanism for translating meeting findings into leadership actions where patterns are systemic.
points: The author's central error was grounding pupil progress meetings in standardised test scores, which measure national norms rather than the school's own taught curriculum — making the data structurally mismatched to the decisions leaders were trying to make.

Scheduling meetings at the end of term (to align with assessment calendars) was a procedural habit with no pedagogical logic: there is no inherent reason for pupil progress conversations to follow standardised testing rather than precede or run independently of it.

The scope error was the most consequential: focusing on children who appeared 'off track' on a progress matrix actively obscured the persistently low-attaining pupils who might fall within the 'on track' band — a systematic blind spot built into the model's own filtering logic.

The meetings, as designed, consumed teacher time using data that couldn't actually drive the conversations teachers needed to have about individual and common barriers to learning — teachers could have had those conversations without the matrices.

Three elements are worth preserving in any revised model: a bank of rules of thumb for common needs, a solution-focused meeting structure, and a clear process for turning identified patterns into systemic leadership action.
quotes: I deluded myself into thinking that I was doing 'decision driven data collection' by thinking: What improvements do we need to make to curriculum / pedagogy / interventions / operations?' and then using standardised test data to help with that decision making. In fact, I was still doing 'data driven decision making'.

Standardised tests are not an assessment of our curriculum. Reading extracts would only match the texts that we've taught by an incredible fluke and although maths tests are written to sample the national curriculum, they're incredibly unlikely to match what we've taught either.

At the time, I thought that using standardised test scores was the right thing to do because it was the most reliable assessment and would allow for the most valid of inferences by virtue of the standardisation and benchmarking against national comparison; a perfect example of misunderstanding the data and using it for something it isn't designed for.

Turns out that none of that was necessary for teachers to talk about the common or individual barriers to greater success. The reality was that the meetings were more for leaders than they were for teachers. We wanted to know how children were doing and contribute to making improvements but we were taking up teachers' time using inadequate information to do it.

meetings yield actions for leaders. This is particularly important if there are obvious patterns in what barriers exist and a common need for certain strategies. If either are systemic, it is leaders' job to tackle it. Even if barriers are not systemic, it is still our responsibility to support and enable colleagues to improve on an individual basis.

Until recently, our model for pupil progress meetings was a termly conversation with a year group at a time. We'd use progress matrices that showed KS1 attainment against the most recent standardised test score in reading and maths as a starting point for identifying children that might need more than we're providing. They'd result in adaptations to curriculum, pedagogy, intervention and operations.
